content.title: COOKING "HEALTHY" MEALS THAT ARE SECRETLY {{WORTHLESS}}
facts: **Boiling broccoli** – Dunking it in water for 10 minutes drains over half its vitamin C into the pot; steam it for 5 minutes instead to keep most of it intact.
**Salad first, dressing later** – Pouring oil-based dressing on at the very end instead of tossing it in means you absorb far less vitamin A, D, E, and K from your veggies.
**Microwaving in plastic** – Reheating leftovers in the same plastic container they came in can leach chemicals into your food, even when it's labeled "microwave-safe."
**Draining and rinsing canned beans too fast** – A quick rinse under the tap washes away sodium, yes, but also some of the soluble fiber sitting in that starchy liquid.

**Overcrowding the pan** – Piling too many vegetables into one pan traps steam instead of letting them sear, so they end up soggy and lose that fat-soluble nutrient boost that comes from light caramelizing.
**Tossing the cooking water** – Pasta and vegetable water holds potassium and B vitamins that leached out during cooking; save a splash for soups or sauces instead of pouring it down the drain.
**Pre-cutting fruit hours ahead** – Slicing melon or apples long before eating exposes more surface area to air, speeding up nutrient loss and oxidation.

**Cooking everything at high heat** – Blasting delicate oils like olive oil on high heat breaks them down into compounds your body doesn't want; save the high heat for sturdier oils and keep olive oil for finishing.

content.caption:
Let's talk about a few of these mistakes, because the "why" matters more than the rule itself. Boiling broccoli seems harmless, but vitamin C is water-soluble and heat-sensitive, so every minute it sits in hot water is a minute it's leaching out and literally dissolving into the liquid you're about to dump. Dressing timing with your salad matters because vitamins A, D, E, and K need fat to be absorbed into your bloodstream at all — without oil touching the leaves early on, a chunk of those nutrients just passes through you unused. And overcrowding the pan isn't just a texture issue: when vegetables steam instead of sear, they release more water-soluble nutrients into that puddle at the bottom of the pan instead of keeping them locked inside. Everyone's kitchen setup is different, so adjust at your own pace.
